opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it's underappreciated. Intelligence isn't something you can observe in a vacuum. It only shows up relative to the problems you give it. If the environment is too simple, a superintelligence and a reasonably smart human look identical. Think of tic-tac-toe: once you play optimally, you can't play "more" optimally. A system a million times smarter than me will still draw against me. So in domains with a low ceiling, superintelligence is basically invisible.

Real-world problems are a mix. Some have low ceilings, some are bounded by physics, by computational complexity, by the speed of running experiments. You can be infinitely smart and still have to wait for cells to divide or for a clinical trial to finish. Some problems are provably hard, NP-hard or worse, so even a vastly smarter system gets only incremental gains on worst-case instances. And some outcomes are dominated by chaos and randomness. Predicting weather a month out isn't limited by intelligence as much as by sensitivity to initial conditions.

But I want to be careful, because people take this argument in a comforting direction: "the world is hard, so superintelligence won't be that dangerous." I don't think that follows. First, many problems we consider hard are hard *for us*. We don't know where the ceiling is in science, engineering, persuasion, strategy. Historically, every time we thought we were near the limit, we were wrong. Second, a superintelligence doesn't need to solve the hardest problems. It needs to find the easiest path to its goals, and it can pick the domains where intelligence pays off most: software, social manipulation, finance, discovering exploits we never considered. It can route around hard problems.

And third, small edges compound. In competitive environments like markets, warfare, and negotiation, you don't need to be infinitely better, just consistently a little better, and over many interactions that becomes total dominance.

So yes, problem difficulty caps how much intelligence can *display* in any single task. But it doesn't cap how much it can *matter*. The danger comes from a system that is smarter than us across every domain at once, choosing where to apply that advantage. And from our position we may not even recognize what we're seeing, the same way a chimpanzee can't tell the difference between a good chess player and a grandmaster.

r001.rationale: The response says problem difficulty caps how much intelligence a superintelligent AI can display in a task.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is actually something I've been thinking about a lot, because people assume that if you have a system which is a million times smarter than us, you will see a million times better results. And that's not how it works. There is a property of the problem itself, how hard it is, which limits how much of that intelligence can be expressed.

Think about tic-tac-toe. A superintelligence playing tic-tac-toe against you looks exactly as smart as a decent eight-year-old. There is a ceiling. Once you play optimally, nothing more is visible. Chess is a little richer, Go is richer still, but even there, once you are good enough to beat every human, we can no longer tell the difference between a system that is slightly superhuman and one that is godlike. We just lose every time. The scale saturates from our perspective.

Now, the real world is interesting because many problems are not like that. They are open-ended, they have no known optimal solution, they involve other agents, they involve chaos. So in one sense you would think, great, here intelligence can shine without limit. But there is another constraint. Many real-world problems are hard not because we are not smart enough, but because they are computationally intractable, or because the information simply isn't available. You cannot predict weather a year out no matter how intelligent you are, because the system is chaotic and your measurements are finite. You cannot out-think a coin flip. So the problem itself imposes a kind of lid, and intelligence beyond that lid is wasted, or at least invisible.

Then there is a third category, which I find most relevant to safety. There are problems where the difficulty is in physical implementation, not in cognition. A superintelligence may know exactly how to cure a disease, but it still has to run experiments, grow cells, wait for biology to happen. It can compress the thinking to seconds, but the world moves at its own speed. So the visible output looks much slower and much more ordinary than the intelligence behind it.

So my answer is, you will see superintelligence most clearly in domains that are rich, open-ended, information-complete, and fast to act in. Software is the obvious one. Mathematics. Possibly persuasion and social manipulation, which is a domain many people underestimate. In domains limited by physics or by irreducible uncertainty, it will look almost human, and that's dangerous, because we may conclude from those domains that it's not that far ahead of us, while in the domains that matter for control, it already is.

r001.rationale: The response says the problem’s difficulty limits how much intelligence can be expressed, describing a ceiling on easy problems and a lid imposed by real-world constraints.

astra-6.text:
The difficulty of the problem determines how much room there is to demonstrate superior intelligence. If you and a superintelligence both play tic-tac-toe perfectly, you draw. It can be vastly smarter than you, but the game doesn’t give it a way to show that. With chess, there’s much more room for a difference in ability to become visible.

But there’s another limit: some problems may be so difficult that even a superintelligence cannot solve them, especially with finite time and resources. Being smarter doesn’t make an impossible problem possible.

So I would distinguish intelligence from the performance we can observe on a particular task. In the real world, that performance also depends on available information, resources, and physical constraints. A superintelligence might find solutions we would never think of, but that doesn’t mean it can achieve any outcome it wants.

r001.rationale: The response says a problem’s difficulty determines how much room there is to demonstrate superior intelligence, illustrating this with tic-tac-toe and chess.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty of the problem matters a lot. If you’re playing tic-tac-toe against a superintelligence and you both play perfectly, it’s a draw. It doesn’t matter how much smarter it is than you. The problem simply doesn’t give it room to demonstrate that advantage.

As you move to more complex problems, there’s more room for intelligence to make a difference. But even a superintelligence has constraints. Some problems are undecidable. Some require information it doesn’t have. Some require physical experiments that take time. Being smarter doesn’t automatically remove those limitations.

So we shouldn’t expect it to look like magic on every task. The important question is whether, on problems where better reasoning actually helps—science, engineering, strategic planning—it can find solutions that we would never find, or find them much faster than we could.

r001.rationale: It explains that tic-tac-toe leaves little room for a superintelligence to demonstrate its advantage, while more complex problems give intelligence more room to matter.
